## What Is Coopetition?

> *"Business is cooperation when it comes to creating a pie and competition when it comes to dividing it up."*
> — Nalebuff & Brandenburger

**Coopetition** = **Co**operation + Com**petition**

A strategic mindset that rejects the zero-sum view of business:

- Traditional view: competitors are enemies, industry is a battlefield
- Coopetition view: rivals can **simultaneously cooperate and compete**
- Rooted in **game theory** — specifically, the theory of *value nets* and *complementors*

::: {.callout-note}
Published in 1996, *Co-opetition* by Adam Brandenburger (Harvard) and Barry Nalebuff (Yale) became a landmark business strategy text.
:::

---

## The Value Net Framework

The **Value Net** maps all players in the game of business:

```
            CUSTOMERS
                |
SUPPLIERS — [COMPANY] — COMPETITORS
                |
         COMPLEMENTORS
```

| Player | Role |
|---|---|
| **Customers** | Buy your product or service |
| **Suppliers** | Provide inputs to your business |
| **Competitors** | Offer substitutes; divide the pie |
| **Complementors** | Offer complements; **grow** the pie |

::: {.callout-tip}
**Key insight:** The same player can be a competitor *and* a complementor depending on context.
:::

---

## Complementors — The Core Concept

A firm is your **complementor** if customers value your product *more* when they also have the other firm's product.

A firm is your **competitor** if customers value your product *less* when they also have the other firm's product.

**Classic examples:**

| Your Product | Complementor | Why? |
|---|---|---|
| Hardware (PC) | Software (Windows) | Each makes the other more valuable |
| Cars | Petrol stations | More stations → more car purchases |
| Video game console | Game titles | More games → more console sales |
| Credit cards | Merchants who accept cards | Each side needs the other |

::: {.callout-important}
Complementors **grow the total pie** — this is where coopetition creates value before competition divides it.
:::

---

## PARTS — The Five Elements of Strategy

Nalebuff & Brandenburger propose **PARTS** as levers to change the game:

| Letter | Element | Question |
|---|---|---|
| **P** | Players | Who is in the game? Can we add/remove players? |
| **A** | Added Values | What do we uniquely bring? |
| **R** | Rules | What governs the game? Can we reshape them? |
| **T** | Tactics | How do perceptions shape behavior? |
| **S** | Scope | What is the boundary of the game? |

::: {.callout-note}
**Strategy = changing the game**, not just playing it well. PARTS gives managers a systematic toolkit to identify where and how to intervene.
:::

---

## Example: Intel & Microsoft (Wintel)

**The classic coopetition case**

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Cooperation
- Intel and Microsoft are **complementors**: faster chips → demand for richer software; better software → demand for faster chips
- Both invest heavily in growing the PC market
- Joint marketing ("Intel Inside" + Windows branding)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Competition
- Both are large enough to **capture the other's value**
- Microsoft delayed 64-bit OS support, slowing Intel's upgrade cycle
- Intel promoted rival OS vendors (e.g., Linux) to reduce Microsoft's leverage
- Each tried to expand into the other's domain
:::

::::

::: {.callout-tip}
**Lesson:** Even the closest complementors compete over value appropriation. Cooperation and rivalry coexist permanently.
:::

---

## Example: Airline Alliances (Star Alliance, Oneworld)

**Cooperation on routes, competition on price and loyalty**

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
### Cooperation
- Code-sharing: airlines sell seats on each other's flights
- Shared lounges, baggage handling, and check-in
- Coordinated schedules to expand network reach
- Joint lobbying on aviation regulations
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
### Competition
- Head-to-head rivalry on overlapping routes
- Competing frequent-flyer programs
- Price wars on transatlantic and transpacific corridors
- Alliance partners compete for corporate contracts
:::

::::

::: {.callout-note}
**Value Net lens:** Alliance partners are **complementors** on thin-margin routes neither could serve alone, and **competitors** on profitable trunk routes.
:::

---

## Example: Apple vs. Samsung

**Supplier, competitor, and complementor — simultaneously**

- **Supplier:** Samsung manufactures chips (A-series), displays, and memory used in iPhones
- **Competitor:** Samsung Galaxy directly competes with iPhone in smartphones
- **Complementor (indirect):** Samsung's Android ecosystem legitimizes the smartphone category, validating demand that Apple also captures

> Samsung reportedly earned billions annually supplying components to Apple even while competing fiercely in the handset market.

::: {.callout-important}
**Lesson:** Supply relationships and competitive rivalries are not mutually exclusive. The Value Net forces managers to hold both realities at once.
:::

---

## Example: Automotive Industry & Shared R&D

**Competing on brand; cooperating on infrastructure**

| Initiative | Partners | Cooperation | Competition |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bluetooth / USB standards** | All automakers | Agreed on connectors | Compete on in-car UX |
| **Battery recycling consortia** | GM, Ford, VW, etc. | Share recycling infrastructure costs | Compete for EV market share |
| **HERE Maps** | BMW, Audi, Daimler | Co-own mapping platform | Compete on navigation features |
| **Hydrogen fueling stations** | Toyota, Honda, Hyundai | Fund shared station networks | Compete on fuel-cell vehicles |

::: {.callout-tip}
**Pre-competitive cooperation:** Firms cooperate to build the *platform* (grow the pie), then compete to capture value from it.
:::

---

## Example: Video Game Consoles — Nintendo & Third-Party Developers

**A two-sided market coopetition dynamic**

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
### Nintendo Cooperates With Developers
- Licenses its platform and tools to third parties
- Shares marketing support for major releases
- Third-party titles (Ubisoft, EA, Activision) make the Switch more attractive to buyers
- More buyers → more developer revenue → virtuous cycle
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
### Nintendo Competes With Developers
- First-party titles (Mario, Zelda, Pokémon) directly compete for gamers' time and wallets
- Nintendo controls the App Store equivalent — sets fee terms
- Can delay or deny certification to rivals
:::

::::

::: {.callout-note}
**Platform businesses** are structurally coopetitive: the platform owner must attract partners to grow the ecosystem while competing with those same partners for end-user spending.
:::

---

## Key Takeaways

### The Coopetition Mindset

1. **Reject zero-sum thinking** — value can be created before it is divided
2. **Map your Value Net** — identify complementors you may be ignoring
3. **Use PARTS** — you can change the game, not just play it
4. **Embrace ambiguity** — a rival can be an ally on a different dimension
5. **Grow the pie first** — cooperation to expand the market; compete to capture your share

### When Is Coopetition Most Valuable?
- Markets with **network effects** (platforms, ecosystems)
- Industries requiring **shared standards or infrastructure**
- Situations where **neither firm can serve the market alone**
- **Pre-competitive R&D** with uncertain, expensive outcomes

::: {.callout-important}
*"The name of the game is changing the game."* — Brandenburger & Nalebuff
:::
